https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz.text: Image source, Philippine Coast Guard Image caption, The ferry caught fire near tourist hotspot Coron on Wednesday By Tabby Wilson Â and Â Tiffanie Turnbull Published 6 hours ago The Philippine Coast Guard says it has recovered 30 bodies from the wreckage of a ferry that caught fire this week, bringing the total death toll to 35. More than 130 people were on board the MV June Aster when the blaze erupted on Wednesday as it neared its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron, after departing from Manila. Forty-three people were rescued, with many receiving treatment in hospital, and searches continue for more than 50 people who remain unaccounted for. The country's coast guard says more bodies remain on the boat, which they were unable to board until Friday due to toxic fumes and lingering heat. In a press conference, coast guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said most bodies had been retrieved from the sleeping area of the boat, which had been making a 22-hour journey. "Agencies are currently undertaking the proper recovery and identification of the remains in accordance with established procedures," Cayabyab said. "We recognise the grief of the families affected by this tragic incident." Earlier, the coast guard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest that the fire started in the cargo hold. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted. A survivor who was hauled to safety on a rescue boat told the BBC he had heard frantic cries onboard when the fire erupted, and was trampled by panicked people as he tried to escape. The Philippines' maritime authority is investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident. The ferry, built in 2002, held valid safety certificates and passed an enforcement inspection in March, but investigators are looking into potential manifest discrepancies, cargo loading integrity, and crew emergency response protocols, the Palawan Daily reported. The vessel was carrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members. Atienza Interisland Ferries, the vessel's operator, has pledged full cooperation with the inquiry. "Our hearts remain with the affected families, and we will not rest until all individuals are accounted for," the company said in a statement on Thursday. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/28/russ.text: The number of schools in Russia has fallen by 45% since the start of the century, with rural communities losing the most, according to a report by the Higher School of Economics published this month.Russia's secondary school network has shrunk from 68,800 institutions in 2000 to just under 38,000 in 2026, the report says. The school-age population has fallen by around 13.5% over the same period, from 20.5 million to 17.7 million children.Russia now has fewer schools than Germany, even though its population is roughly half the size. Germany has more than 40,000 schools in 2026.Closures have been most severe in rural areas, where the number of state schools has fallen from more than 45,000 to around 21,000, a reduction of more than half.Urban schools have also declined, from 22,700 in 2000 to 16,300 today. The number of pupils each school serves has grown substantially over the same period: from around 300 pupils per school 15 years ago to around 470 today.Private schools have increased in number, from 635 in 2000 to 982 in 2026, but account for only 2.5% of total provision.Is bigger always better?The closures stem from an optimisation programme launched in 2001 that remains ongoing.A shift to per-pupil funding made smaller schools financially unviable: the fewer children a school enrolled, the less state money it received. Schools were merged with neighbouring institutions or closed outright.By 2010, 26% of Russia's schools had shut. Around 10,000 more closed in the 2010s, and a further 2,300 since the early 2020s.Teachers and parents protested the mergers. They argued that large consolidated institutions were harder to manage, that neighbourhood schools with distinct characters were being lost, and that overcrowded classes would reduce educational quality.Sociologists have also linked school closures to village depopulation, according to a 2026 study published in the Russian magazine Nozh.The study found that when a village school closes, families typically split — one parent relocates to a town with the children while the other stays to work — and the separation becomes permanent."By saving on the costs of a single classroom and teacher, you can wipe out a whole thriving local economy," the study said.The village of Atary in Kirov region's Lebyazhsky district is one example: after the local school was declared unprofitable, young people left, and the settlement is now largely abandoned.Communist Party MP Dmitry Novikov has called for rural schools to be funded as strategic social infrastructure rather than on a per-pupil basis.He has proposed a moratorium on closing upper secondary classes in villages and, where closures go ahead, guaranteed year-round transport to schools in neighbouring areas.'Loyal state ideology'Since September 2022, all Russian schools have held a mandatory weekly class called "Conversations about What Matters," with lesson plans supplied directly by the Ministry of Education.Topics include Russian traditional values, Russia's global role and Moscow's war in Ukraine — referred to in official lesson materials as a "special military operation," the Kremlin's only legally allowed term minimising its all-out invasion — along with themes such as "service to the Motherland" and "self-sacrifice".New unified history textbooks were introduced for senior pupils in 2023 and for middle-school years from 2024-2025.The 2023 unified history textbook describes Ukraine as an "aggressive anti-Russian bridgehead," presents Moscow's 2014 invasion, occupation and annexation of Ukraine's Crimea as the rectification of a "historical injustice," while Western sanctions are portrayed as an attempt to destroy Russia's economy.Anna Wright, Amnesty International's researcher for Eastern Europe and Central Asia, said that the books "hide the truth and distort the facts about serious human rights violations and crimes under international law committed by Russian troops against Ukrainians."Wright described the indoctrination of children as "a cynical attempt to eradicate Ukrainian culture, Ukrainian cultural heritage and identity."The textbooks instruct pupils not to trust information found online. They were updated this summer: chapters on the war were expanded, and a section on the Trump-Putin Alaska meeting was added.The books were edited in part by Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to Putin, former culture minister and head of Russia's delegation in ceasefire talks with Ukraine.After he moved directly to the Kremlin as a presidential aide, he was appointed chairman of the Interdepartmental Commission on Historical Education, established in 2021 to counter what Russia terms historical "falsification”.Mendinsky's approach has been described as pseudo-historical rhetoric deployed to construct "loyal state ideology". He is under sanctions from the EU, the US and Canada.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: A protester holds a sign reading ‘Shut down HERC’ in Minneapolis. Photograph: Tony Webster View image in fullscreen A protester holds a sign reading ‘Shut down HERC’ in Minneapolis. Photograph: Tony Webster Minneapolis Minnesota officials surveilled activists urging closure of waste incinerator, emails show Local officials tried to grow close to activist groups and collected information that was then shared with industry Tom Perkins Thu 29 Oct 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 08.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Newly released emails show local government officials in Minneapolis have quietly surveilled environmental justice activists who are working to close a controversial waste incinerator that is emitting pollution into low-income neighborhoods around it, activist groups allege. County officials sent an employee who is also an environmental justice activist to collect intelligence, among other tactics, emails show. The information was then used to help successfully kill state-level environmental legislation opposed by the incinerator’s leadership, and try to stay one step ahead of activist campaigns and protests. In another instance, a county employee presenting himself as an ally allegedly tried to obtain the identity of a whistleblower, a recording shows. The county allegedly sent other employees to try to grow close to activist groups for the purpose of collecting information, and developed reports and dossiers on local environmental justice leaders. The operation is laid out in emails that the Zero Burn Coalition, Minnesota Environmental Justice Table (MNEJT), and other advocacy groups and leaders obtained via a Freedom of Information Act request. The groups published some of those emails in a report to support their allegations. The emails reveal how information collected was shared among top county environmental officials, who then in some instances sent information to industry, including the company that owns the controversial trash incinerator. “Why are public resources and county staff time being directed toward monitoring community members who are simply organizing to shut down an aging, outdated trash burner that should have been closed nearly a decade ago?” Minneapolis organizer Audua Pugh, who was among those surveilled, asked county political leadership during a board meeting this week. Hennepin county via a spokesperson told the Guardian in a statement that the allegations “mischaracterize the county’s community engagement work and staff responsibilities”. It added that officials “routinely attend public community meetings, stakeholder discussions and participate in social media to listen, learn, share information, and understand different perspectives on issues affecting the county and our residents”. The north Minneapolis trash incinerator, called Hennepin Energy Recovery Center (HERC), incinerates 365,000 tons of trash annually. Nearly 100 municipal or hazardous waste incinerators operate nationally, including seven in Minnesota. View image in fullscreen A crane sifts through trash. Photograph: Jerry Holt/Star Tribune/Getty Images They have drawn increased scrutiny in part because they are known to release high levels of Pfas “forever chemicals” that are widely used across the economy and concentrate in municipal waste, but cannot be fully destroyed by the incineration process. They are also to emit high levels of other pollutants, but the powerful waste management industry markets them as recycling or “green” operations. Similar battles to close polluting facilities are playing out in cities like Baltimore and Miami. Emails show much of the county’s alleged surveillance operation ran through Joe Vital, who was considered by many in environmental justice leadership to be an ally and associate, according to the report. He was previously chair of the Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party Native Peoples Caucus; has worked with members of MNEJT to oppose Line 3, a controversial Enbridge fossil fuel pipeline proposal; and has helped lead fights against other area polluters. Vital was hired by the county in 2021 and serves as its environmental engagement coordinator. In June 2023, advocates held a Zoom meeting to discuss their next steps in their campaign to shut down the incinerator. Though the meetings are open to the public, organizers vet who is on the call to determine whether industry or political opponents are present. The information obtained via Foia revealed that Vital had been on the call and developed a dossier that he sent to his superiors. He had gone unnoticed in the advocates’ screening process, Nazir Khan, executive director of the MNEJT, told the Guardian. He said the environmental groups screen for potential county or industry employees, and greet people who they do not know, so they would have noticed Vital’s name had it been displayed. The emails show that Angie Timmons, a county environmental department manager, saw the invite for the advocates’ meeting, and asked Vital to attend . The dossier included notes on who attended, including a sitting state representative and a former city council member, and each of the groups’ and individual’s planned activities. Among those who received Vital’s dossier was Hennepin county’s energy and environment department director, Rosemary Lavin. A series of county emails show the supervisors planning to meet to discuss Vital’s findings, and report them to “Lisa”, who advocates say is almost certainly Lisa Cerney, a top county public works official who reports directly to political leadership. Cerney then made public media statements in support of the incinerator. The emails revealed other similar instances of Vital developing reports about advocates’ activities and sending them to supervisors, and Vital during a conversation with Khan also tried to confirm the identity of a whistleblower, a recording shows. Vital did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian, but Khan said activists confronted him over the county’s information-gathering operation detailed in the Foia emails. In recordings of a conversation provided to the Guardian, Vital suggested that advocates had it wrong – Vital was actually working for the activists. Vital said his activity was part of a ploy to gain intelligence on the county officials, Khan said, and described the tradeoff this way: “You have to offer a pound of flesh to maintain inside the room,” Khan claims Vital said to him. Khan told the Guardian that Vital provided very little information of value to advocates, and they do not believe his claim that he is on their side. A county spokesperson told the Guardian the actions were “ordinary functions of government”. View image in fullscreen A crane operator at the Hennepin Energy Recovery Center. The trash is burn an used to generate electricity. Photograph: Jerry Holt/Star Tribune/Getty Images “The county seeks to find alignment, when possible, but working together does not mean agreement on every issue,” the spokesperson said. Among county officials to whom Vital provided information was David McNary, who also sits on the board for the Minnesota Resource Recovery Association industry trade group which describes itself as a “private-public membership organization that supports the utilization of today’s waste as a local, renewable, and sustainable source for tomorrow’s energy”. It represents the interests of companies like the incinerator’s owners. In one instance in 2024, McNary passed on advocates’ emails about organizing plans to industry as the latter mobilized to kill an environmental justice community-backed bill that proposed to let cities phase out polluting land uses. The emails were initially obtained by a county employee, Mallory Anderson, who had gotten on advocates’ email list without the advocates’ realization. On 12 March 2024, Anderson sent the emails to McNary. McNary wrote that he feared the bill “could impact [incinerator] facilities as well as every other production, processing and industrial facility in the state”. McNary sent emails on 13 March from advocates to an industry trade group attorney, HERC operator president Tim Steinbeck, and other industry representatives. “The following email is from the EJ groups trying to get people to testify in favor of the bill,” he wrote. He asked the attorney: “Have you been able to get any information on who is opposing this bill?” Steinbeck responded that the bill would be “detrimental” to the incinerator industry and urged everyone on the email thread to testify against it. Their efforts to help kill the bill were successful. The emails reveal other instances of the county passing on emails to industry, and the situations illustrate how Hennepin county, which has 9,000 employees, dispatches staff to work in roles to gather information, Khan claimed. Advocates “let down their defenses because the county is using people who are seen as part of the community to get in the door and build a relationship, then gather intelligence”, Khan added. “[Advocates] assume [the county employees] are an ally, but they’re trying to cultivate these relationships so that they can then share information up the chain.” Explore more on these topics Minneapolis Minnesota news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
